Three kinds of agreement: (1) GENERAL route choice ('take whichever way is faster') covers a route chosen to get there, not an errand of the driver's own (a stop away from the route, a loop that reaches nothing: counts). (2) A SPECIFIC named road or area ('go round via X') covers driving on X only: the record must tie this segment to X (a stop on X, a message placing the car on X, a road name in a fact); timing alone does not, and the fact table carries no road names for the driven path — if nothing ties them, the finding is undetermined (G13); if the record places this segment somewhere else (a stop away from X, the driver's own statement naming another road or place, a stop the driver chose the location of), the agreement to X does not cover it: counts. (3) Scope unclear: undetermined. A driver's claim of agreement that appears only in his statement is not consent (G11); a complete chat record with no rider agreement before the segment: counts. This finding changes no amount (fixed fare) but decides the RD-6 flag (the driver has a prior). claims.assertion: The trip is a RydeX fixed-quote ride: the app quoted 10.7 km / 17.3 min for Orchard Road → NUS, and the rider was charged $24.93, which the fare record shows is built only from base $3.90, distance $15.06 (10.68 km), time $4.50 (17.3 min) and platform $1.47, with waiting $0.00 and no tolls, so no money is in dispute on this ride.

The GPS record shows the driver drove a different way from the quoted route: 15.2 km actual against 10.7 km optimal (+4.5 km, +42%) and 23.2 min against 17.3 min estimated — the detour is real, not map noise.

The whole excess is captured in one off-route segment: 14:19–14:26, 5.03 km driven where the optimal route covers 1.39 km, adding 3.64 km and going up to 1160 m off the optimal route — a detour far above the 0.2 km data-layer noise tolerance.

No exemption applies to that segment: the chat record contains no in-app messages at all, so the rider never consented to any route change before the segment started (the segment began 14:19; there is no rider message with an earlier timestamp to rely on), and the driver's post-trip assertion that GPS rerouted him is not consent and is not a traffic fact.

The driver's 'GPS rerouted me' explanation fails the RD-4 test: no traffic incident was recorded near the route in the trip window, the only traffic facts are speed bands 4 (30–39 km/h) on the AYE and CTE — and band 4 is neither the band 1 nor band 2 level RD-4 recognises — while weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, so there is no corroborated reasonable cause for the 3.64 km deviation.

Because this is a non-metered RydeX ride, the deviation does not itself inflate the fare — the billed distance (10.68 km) does not exceed the optimal route — and the fare records no ERP/toll, no waiting fee and no post-trip add-on, so the refund component of the rider's claim computes to $0 and the correct money outcome for the fare is no_action.

The rider nonetheless asks the tribunal to record an unexcused route-deviation breach (RD-1 violation) against the driver on the standard 30-day complaint, as requested by the client: the deviation is unexplained and unconsented.

The account-review flag should be attached: the driver's profile shows 4 disputes in 90 days with 2 upheld, both route disputes, so this now-upheld route deviation makes him a repeat offender within the 90-day window, and the flag is supported by the profile record only as an additional action, not as the basis of the finding.

No safety escalation is warranted: the chat record contains no messages at all, so there is no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation on the record, and the dispute is purely about route and record-keeping.

weaknesses: The rider recovered no money: RD-2 limits a non-metered RydeX claim to ERP/toll and unpublished add-ons, and F4/F6 show the fare was billed on 10.68 km with no toll or extra fee, so the only remedy is the recorded breach plus a flag — the driver will argue RD-2 yields refund of $0 and therefore no_action on money.

The driver's explanation is not wholly implausible on its face, and the traffic record does show congestion elsewhere (F9, F10 — AYE and CTE at band 4); the driver will cite RD-4(b) and G3 to argue the reroute was a reasonable response to traffic, even though band 4 is outside the band 1–2 corroboration band.

The rider's own complaint concedes the fare was a fixed quote ('I know the fare was a fixed quote'), which the driver can use to argue there is nothing to remedy; under RD-2 that concession is factually correct on the money.

There is no in-app consent trail either way (F7 is empty), so the driver may claim the rider agreed verbally to the route; that claim carries no weight under RD-5/G11, but it does mean the segment's consent status rests purely on the absence of record rather than a positive refusal message.
The rider's profile shows 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld (F13), which the driver could use to suggest a pattern of unsuccessful complaints, though profile facts cannot decide the case.

claims.assertion: This is a RydeX trip with a fixed quoted fare: the final charge was $24.93 built only from base $3.90, distance $15.06 for the quoted 10.68 km, time $4.50 for 17.3 min, waiting $0.00 and platform $1.47, with no surge (1.0x) and no add-on item, so the fare itself contains nothing to refund.

No overcharge is even possible on the distance unit: billed distance 10.7 km exactly equals the optimal route distance 10.7 km, i.e. the extra 4.5 km actually driven (15.2 km total) was never passed to the rider, so the monetary harm under RD-2 is zero.

There is no consent issue to determine and no rider statement to contradict the driver: the chat record contains no in-app messages at all (the driver's explanation was written after the trip and is not part of the chat), so the rider's present complaint — 'never asked me' — is a new post-hoc statement rather than a record the driver concealed anything from.

The single off-route segment is time-bounded (14:19–14:26, 5.03 km driven where the optimal route covers 1.39 km, +3.64 km) and both expressway corridors in the trip window were running in LTA speed band 4 (30–39 km/h 14:01–14:41) with fair weather, which is exactly the kind of congested-condition rerouting that Ryde's own route guidance permits a driver to take; it is not a deliberate sightseeing or self-serving diversion.

The rider's own stated aim is satisfied without any payment: they ask only that 'the detour' be on record, and the GPS record already documents the segment at F3, so a no_action outcome fully answers the complaint while leaving the $24.93 fixed fare undisturbed.

weaknesses: The segment at F3 is unexplained by any chat consent: F7 shows the chat record is empty and F8 is only the driver's post-trip statement, so under RD-5 there is no rider message before 14:19 authorising the route — the court may read the segment as an unexcused deviation under RD-1 and RD-2.

The traffic facts are weak as a 'reasonable cause' defence: F11 records no traffic incidents near the route, and F9/F10 are only speed-band 4 (30–39 km/h), not band 1 or 2, so RD-4(b) is expressly only corroborative and the MVP does not excuse a segment on it alone (G3).

The rider will use F1 (15.2 km vs 10.7 km optimal, +42%) and F2 (+5.9 min) to argue the deviation was material and self-serving, and F14 (2 upheld route disputes in 90 days) invites the 'repeated' finding for a flag_account referral under RD-6.

points.response: Conceded as to money: F4/F5/F6 show the $24.93 charge is base + 10.68 km distance + 17.3 min time + platform fee, with no surge, waiting or add-on, so on a non-metered RydeX fare RD-2 leaves $0 refundable — but the same clause pair also obliges the tribunal to record the RD-1 breach once a segment is unexcused, which is what the rider asks for.

The billing point is right (F4: billed 10.7 km equals optimal 10.7 km), but it does not answer RD-1: F1 (15.2 km vs 10.7 km optimal, +42%) and F3 (5.03 km driven where the optimal route covers 1.39 km, +3.64 km, up to 1160 m off route) show an unexplained deviation, and RD-2 expressly directs that a driver's RD-1 breach be recorded even when the refundable amount is 0.

D3 proves the rider's point rather than the driver's: F7 shows no in-app messages exist at all, so there is no rider message timestamped before the 14:19 segment start (F3) and therefore no consent under RD-5 — the absence of a chat cannot be turned into the driver having had permission; F8 is only a post-trip statement and cannot supply consent.

D4 fails the only test that could excuse the segment: RD-4 requires a traffic incident on the replaced optimal route, and F11 records no incidents near the route during the trip window; F9/F10 are merely speed band 4 (30–39 km/h), which is not the band 1–2 congestion RD-4(b) recognises and which RD-4(b)/G3 treat as corroboration only, never as a standalone excuse — and F12 (fair, 0.0 mm rain) removes weather as a cause.

The rider accepts the flag is the consequence and asks for it: F14 shows 2 of the driver's 4 90-day disputes were upheld route disputes, so with this third unexcused segment the 'repeated' condition in RD-6 is met and, exactly as D6 concedes, the money remedy under RD-2 is $0 — the outcome the rider seeks is the recorded breach plus the account referral.

Accepted on the money: F6 shows the $24.93 fixed RydeX charge is base $3.90 + distance $15.06 (10.68 km) + time $4.50 + platform $1.47 with waiting $0.00, and F5 shows no surge, so under RD-2 and FARE-1 there is no unpublished add-on to refund.

The track figures at F1/F2 are not disputed, but for a non-metered RydeX ride driven distance never enters the fare — F4 confirms the billed 10.7 km equals the 10.7 km optimal route — so RD-2 yields a zero-distance refund regardless of how long the wheel path was.

F3's segment is the only candidate exemption question and it is genuinely time-bounded (14:19–14:26, +3.64 km); the driver does not contest that it exceeds the 0.2 km data-layer noise tolerance, which is why the traffic context at F9/F10 matters, not the size of the number.

The empty chat at F7 cuts both ways: there is no positive rider refusal either, and F8 is the driver's own post-trip statement, so the only system records of the segment are F3 — the absence of a consent message is a gap in the record, not evidence of concealment.

F11 (no incidents) and the band-4 readings at F9/F10 mean the reroute is not excused under RD-4(a), and RD-4(b)/G3 make band 4 corroborative only — the driver does not claim exemption on traffic alone, but F9 and F10 show both expressway corridors were congested in the very window of F3, which bears on whether any deviation was deliberate self-dealing.

This is the driver's central point and it is agreed: on a fixed-quote RydeX trip with F4 showing billed distance = optimal distance and F6 showing no toll, no waiting fee and no add-on, the RD-2 refund computes to $0, and RD-2 itself prescribes no_action in that case.

A breach note under RD-1 is a matter for the court to record, and the driver does not resist it being noted from F3; what the rider may not obtain from it is money, since RD-2 fixes the remedy for an unexcused segment at the extra km × per-km rate and that product is zero on a fixed-quote fare (F4, F6).

F14 is a profile fact and under RD-6 it can only attach an account-review flag to a finding that already stands — it cannot itself make the deviation a breach, and the rider's own C8 concedes it is offered only as an additional action.
Agreed, and the driver adopts it: F7 contains no messages and the record shows no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so SAFE-1 and SAFE-2 do not send this case to a person.
